approach.lead: Every engagement starts with a question, not a solution. My practice is built on six principles that guide how I work with organizations facing strategic complexity — from reframing the right problem to designing the conditions for lasting change.
principles: I distill complex ideas into clear, focused narratives that inspire action and transformation. Through storytelling, I connect deeply with audiences and drive change by making the essential visible and memorable.

I treat design as a shared process, working closely with communities to build solutions rooted in their realities. This inclusive approach leads to more meaningful, sustainable, and accepted outcomes.
By embracing systems thinking, I design with awareness of the broader context—linking organizational dynamics, user needs, and societal forces to enable lasting, systemic impact.
I help organizations look beyond the present, designing future-ready solutions that build resilience and ensure relevance in an ever-changing world.
Through fast prototyping and iterative testing, I turn ideas into validated solutions quickly—accelerating learning, adaptation, and measurable innovation.
I design custom strategies that fit the challenge—not templates. By reframing problems and integrating systemic, human-centered thinking, I unlock meaningful and context-driven solutions.

projects.title: OPEX Rates Design Sprint
projects.sub: From fragmented calculations to a more reliable decision-making system
projects.excerpt: Design Sprint & Problem Framing. I facilitated a three-day Design Sprint in Bogotá with more than 20 Ecopetrol participants. On the first day, we aligned the group around the challenge, defined the long-term goal and…
projects.html:
01 —Situation — The Challenge

Ecopetrol’s OPEX rate calculation process relied heavily on manual work, fragmented data sources, individual spreadsheets, and different calculation criteria across teams. This made the process harder to trace, standardize, and scale, while limiting the time analysts could dedicate to higher-value analysis. The challenge was to rethink a critical part of the process and explore how a single, more reliable tool could connect data, standardize calculations, strengthen traceability, and better support Portfolio, Reserves, and FMV processes.

02 —Task — My Role

I led the engagement end to end, directing the multidisciplinary team responsible for research, synthesis, facilitation, prototyping, and strategic definition. I designed and facilitated the three-day Design Sprint with Ecopetrol, guiding a group of more than 20 participants through problem framing, prioritization, ideation, concept development, and validation. I also led the integration of user needs, process requirements, governance considerations, and technical feasibility into a coherent solution and implementation roadmap.

03 —Action — The Process

Immersion & Process Mapping. I led the team through an initial planning phase that included 13 interviews with stakeholders across Ecopetrol, a detailed mapping of the OPEX rate calculation process, and a review of the main tools involved, including SAP, VALNAV, Spotfire, and Planning Space. This allowed us to identify the main barriers around manual work, data access, traceability, methodological consistency, scalability, and the absence of a single source of truth.

Design Sprint & Problem Framing. I facilitated a three-day Design Sprint in Bogotá with more than 20 Ecopetrol participants. On the first day, we aligned the group around the challenge, defined the long-term goal and Sprint focus, explored relevant references, and generated initial concepts. This resulted in five prioritized solution modules: pre-comparison, normalization, escalation, rate visualization, and reporting.

Co-Design & Prototyping. I guided the team through the detailed development of the five modules, defining flows, interaction logic, and key design decisions. In parallel, we worked with the technology team on feasibility and architecture considerations, while another workstream explored process governance, roles, knowledge continuity, and data management. These inputs were consolidated into a high-fidelity prototype that represented a more integrated and traceable end-to-end experience.

Validation with Stakeholders. On the final day, we tested the prototype with key stakeholders from different areas of Ecopetrol and used their feedback to refine the solution. The validation reinforced the value of reducing operational effort so that analysts could spend more time challenging assumptions, working closer to operations, and strengthening process assurance rather than managing manual consolidation.

From Prototype to Implementation. After the Sprint, I led the consolidation of the final prototype, backlog, and implementation roadmap. The solution was structured into three waves: an MVP focused on the core calculation workflow, a functional expansion including visualization and reporting, and a complementary phase introducing AI-assisted capabilities and further automation.

04 —Result

The Sprint transformed a complex operational challenge into a validated product concept, a prioritized backlog, and a clear path toward implementation. The team aligned around a shared vision for a more standardized, traceable, and scalable process, with five core modules and more than 20 key functionalities defined during the engagement. Most importantly, the work reframed automation not simply as a way to reduce manual effort, but as a means to free analysts to focus on judgment, operational insight, and stronger decision-making.

projects.title: Connected Compass
projects.sub: Turning operational expertise into a strategic growth system
projects.excerpt: Leadership Co-Creation. We brought the LATAM leadership team together for a full-day co-creation workshop, followed by focused working sessions with commercial, operations, talent, marketing, and other business…
projects.html:
01 —Situation — The Challenge

MTS LATAM had built a strong position managing real estate assets across five Latin American markets, supported by decades of operational experience, a broad institutional client base, and millions of square meters under management. Yet much of that expertise remained invisible: clients primarily recognized MTS for its execution capabilities, while its strategic knowledge, proprietary operational data, and broader portfolio of services were less visible. The challenge was to clarify where the company had a defensible right to win and translate its existing strengths into a focused path for long-term growth.

02 —Task — My Role

I contributed to a five-week strategic immersion designed to help MTS leadership make clearer choices about where to play, how to win, and what capabilities would be required to sustain its next stage of growth. My work connected research, leadership perspectives, business strategy, brand positioning, and organizational implications into a coherent strategic framework. I also helped translate those choices into a system that could guide prioritization across markets, capabilities, and marketing activation.

03 —Action

Discovery & Strategic Diagnosis. We began by reviewing internal commercial and marketing plans, competitive benchmarks, and existing strategic materials. This was complemented by in-depth interviews with leaders across executive management, commercial, operations, talent, and asset management, allowing us to surface recurring tensions around positioning, growth, organizational habits, technology, and client relationships.

Leadership Co-Creation. We brought the LATAM leadership team together for a full-day co-creation workshop, followed by focused working sessions with commercial, operations, talent, marketing, and other business functions. Rather than treating the engagement as an external diagnosis, the process used the organization’s own experience to turn tensions into explicit strategic choices and create shared ownership of the direction.

Strategic Choices & Positioning. The work clarified priority client profiles and markets, areas the company should deliberately avoid, and a differentiated competitive position: not a traditional operator and not a detached advisory firm, but a strategic operator combining execution with decision-making intelligence. We also connected this position to MTS’s operational data and technology platform, reframing them from supporting infrastructure into evidence of a harder-to-replicate competitive advantage.

Designing the Growth System. We synthesized the strategy into a five-part Property Intelligence Flywheel: protect the operational base, transform data into intelligence, use that intelligence to guide decisions, capture the value created, and expand the company’s reach. Four parallel accelerators—deeper data, increasing switching costs, accumulated reputation, and institutionalized relational capital—showed how the system could strengthen over time rather than operate as a linear strategic plan.

From Strategy to Activation. Finally, we translated the model into three horizons: strengthening the established core, expanding validated markets, and treating new-market opportunities as disciplined experiments. We also reviewed the existing marketing plan against the new strategy, identifying gaps in geographic priorities, audience segmentation, narrative architecture, technology activation, measurement, and governance. This created a clearer bridge between strategic intent and execution.

04 —Result — The Impact

The Connected Compass gave MTS a shared strategic language for connecting operations, proprietary knowledge, brand, market priorities, and organizational capabilities. Instead of pursuing growth as a collection of disconnected initiatives, leadership gained a coherent system for deciding what to strengthen now, what to expand next, and what to explore with greater discipline.

The work also reframed one of the company’s most important assets: its operational footprint was not simply evidence of scale, but the foundation of an intelligence advantage that could inform both client decisions and future differentiation.

projects.sub: Aligning Innovation and Technology with Ecopetrol’s 2040 Vision

projects.html:
01 —Context

In March 2025, Ecopetrol partnered with The Cocktail to host a two-day management workshop in Bucaramanga for the leaders of the Vice Presidency of Technology and Innovation (VTI). The workshop aimed to strengthen team cohesion and define strategic priorities aligned with Ecopetrol's 2040 Strategy. Given the challenges of energy transition and declining sector returns, strengthening VTI's position as a key driver of digital and technological transformation became essential.

02 —The Challenge

The primary challenge was to align VTI's priorities with Ecopetrol Group's strategic objectives while addressing low profitability, internal distrust, and disconnection between business units and technology. VTI needed to establish itself as a strategic partner—one capable of anticipating challenges, delivering tangible value, and setting benchmarks in science, technology, and innovation.

03 —The Process

The workshop followed a three-phase methodology: planning, execution, and reporting. During the planning phase, interviews with key stakeholders informed the design of interactive activities tailored to address VTI’s needs. Over two days, participants engaged in exercises to align on VTI’s purpose, identify cross-cutting challenges, and co-create solutions.

  • Day one focused on understanding Ecopetrol’s strategic context, defining VTI’s vision, and mapping barriers across five strategic focus areas.
  • On day two, these barriers were grouped into four "territories of opportunity," such as improving trust in VTI and enhancing synergies between business and technology.

Participants then developed actionable solutions and detailed lines of action to address these opportunities. The final phase involved documenting results, including a roadmap for implementation and insights to guide future actions.

  • Conducted interviews with key Ecopetrol stakeholders to refine the workshop methodology.
  • Designed and prepared tailored workshop materials.
  • Facilitated two days of in-person collaborative sessions with 17+ managers and leaders.
  • Identified organizational gaps and mapped 17 opportunity areas.
  • Consolidated 4 cross-cutting strategic opportunity territories.
  • Co-created solutions and initiatives for each opportunity area.
  • Defined 12 action lines with detailed planning cards to guide VTI efforts for 2025.

04 —The Impact

The workshop resulted in a clear articulation of VTI’s purpose: leveraging science, technology, and innovation to address Ecopetrol’s most critical challenges while driving efficiency, competitiveness, and sustainability.

Four strategic territories of opportunity were identified, along with corresponding lines of action, such as improving governance, fostering collaboration, and optimizing talent management. These outcomes laid the groundwork for VTI to become a more credible, integrated, and strategically aligned partner within Ecopetrol. Additionally, the initiative highlighted the importance of closing gaps between business and technology, ensuring that VTI evolves from a service provider to a strategic enabler in Ecopetrol’s energy transition journey.

es.sub: Alinear innovación y tecnología con la visión 2040 de Ecopetrol

projects.title: Redefining Core Capabilities
projects.sub: Strategic Priorities for Innovation and Portfolio Management at Ecopetrol
projects.html:
01 —The Context

In February 2025, Ecopetrol, in collaboration with The Cocktail, held a participatory workshop to support the Innovation and Portfolio Management Office (GIP) in aligning its strategic planning with Ecopetrol's 2040 vision. The initiative brought together the three core departments—Planning & Portfolio, Technological Architecture, and Innovation—to collectively define critical capabilities, reflect on their roles, and propose a roadmap to activate these capacities to enhance Ecopetrol's technological transformation and energy transition.

02 —The Challenge

GIP faced several strategic challenges: aligning its initiatives with Ecopetrol’s broader 2040 Strategy, breaking down silos between departments, identifying and enhancing critical capabilities, and fostering a shared sense of purpose. Internal fragmentation, bureaucratic barriers, and resistance to change were limiting the effectiveness and agility needed to drive innovation across the organization.

03 —The Process

The workshop followed a structured three-phase methodology: planning, execution, and reporting. During the planning phase, interviews with stakeholders and a review of existing processes informed the design of the workshop agenda and materials. The one-day session began with an introduction to the roles of each department, followed by collaborative exercises to define GIP’s purpose and co-create its core capabilities. Participants identified eight critical capabilities, such as future visioning, technological exploration, and ecosystem connection, and analyzed their enablers and barriers. The final phase involved documenting the results, including the defined purpose, capabilities, and initial priorities, and preparing recommendations for next steps.

  • Conducted alignment and expectation-setting sessions with stakeholders.
  • Reviewed current processes and opportunities for improvement.
  • Facilitated a co-creation workshop with 50+ participants from GIP’s three departments.
  • Defined a unified purpose and five key strategic capabilities for GIP.
  • Mapped enablers and barriers to capability development.

04 —The Impact

The workshop resulted in a clear articulation of GIP’s purpose: to orchestrate and drive innovation and technological transformation across Ecopetrol, contributing to a more sustainable, competitive, and prosperous energy future. Eight critical capabilities were identified, providing a foundation for GIP’s strategic framework. The session also highlighted key barriers, such as siloed operations and resistance to change, and emphasized the need for cultural shifts to foster innovation. Moving forward, the outcomes will guide the development of strategic priorities, roadmaps, and activation models to ensure GIP’s alignment with Ecopetrol’s 2040 goals while maximizing value for stakeholders.

projects.title: Strategic CX Transformation for Itaú Colombia
projects.html:
01 —The Context

Itaú Colombia is undergoing a strategic shift to become a “future-ready” bank, where digitalization, personalization, and competitiveness are central to growth. To support this vision, the organization engaged in a comprehensive diagnostic process to assess its current customer experience (CX) and define a roadmap for its transformation. I participated in this journey as a CX Lead, supporting the strategic design and coordination of this transformation effort.

02 —The Challenge

Despite its strong positioning in the region, Itaú lagged behind local and international competitors in terms of digital experience—particularly in retail banking. Mobile app instability, UX issues, and missing key functionalities impacted customer satisfaction. The core challenge was to build a transformation model that integrated business needs, customer expectations, and competitive insights to drive a differentiated CX strategy.

03 —The Process

  • Conducted a strategic diagnosis of Itaú’s digital products and current experience ecosystem (AS-IS).
  • Benchmarked more than 30 financial players (traditional banks, fintechs, and neobanks).
  • Defined experience drivers across segments (retail and corporate) to identify opportunities.
  • Mapped gaps in CX performance and contrasted them with best practices and user needs.
  • Created a CX transformation model integrating personalization, multiexperience, agility, and innovation.
  • Designed a future-oriented roadmap based on strategic opportunities and business priorities.
  • Provided evidence-based recommendations for experience evolution across channels and touchpoints.

04 —My Role

As the CX Lead, my role was to accompany and guide the team throughout the strategic definition of Itaú’s new customer experience. I provided coaching to the internal designer to enhance their leadership and strategic thinking, while also offering experience frameworks, inspirational cases, and competitive benchmarks to enrich the design process. I supported the identification of experience drivers and the construction of a transformation model that considered the business, the customer, and the competitive landscape. My involvement was also key in aligning cross-functional teams—business, UX, tech—around a shared vision, and in shaping a clear narrative that connected the current challenges with the desired future state for Itaú’s experience.

projects.sub: Strategic Technology Foresight Model for Ecopetrol
projects.excerpt: VTI (Vice Presidency of Technology and Innovation) held a strategic role for the company's future but needed to strengthen its foresight and technology surveillance capabilities to better connect emerging trends with…
projects.html:
01 —Situation

Ecopetrol faced unprecedented transformation challenges in the global energy sector, requiring strategic diversification toward low-emission electrons and molecules businesses. The company's recent strategic definitions aimed at becoming a business group focused on rentability, efficiency, growth, and sustainability, demanding increasingly robust approaches to anticipate technological and market changes.

VTI (Vice Presidency of Technology and Innovation) held a strategic role for the company's future but needed to strengthen its foresight and technology surveillance capabilities to better connect emerging trends with long-term strategic decisions.

The diagnostic revealed VTI's "vulnerable" position—operating in high environmental volatility but with insufficient future preparedness—characterized by fragmented governance, reactive short-term mindsets, and disconnected strategic planning between corporate strategy, technology roadmaps, and portfolio management.

02 —Task

I led the design and development of an actionable CT+I (Science, Technology, and Innovation) foresight model that would transform VTI into a key enabler of Ecopetrol's Science & Technology strategy. My role encompassed strategic facilitation across three phases: immersion and diagnosis, collaborative intention definition, and detailed model specification with implementation roadmap.

Working alongside cross-functional teams from VTI, ICPET, and business units, I orchestrated a collaborative transformation process that engaged 60+ stakeholders through surveys, interviews, and intensive co-creative workshops to institutionalize systematic technology anticipation capabilities and establish a shared transformative purpose.

03 —Action

First, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of existing foresight practices through a multi-method diagnostic approach that combined stakeholder interviews, document analysis, and organizational survey.

The 16+ in-depth interviews spanned key roles across VTI's leadership including planning and portfolio management, digital architecture, innovation teams, and business partners, alongside strategic voices from ICPET and corporate strategy. These conversations revealed fragmented approaches to technology anticipation, with each area operating different methodologies and timelines without systematic coordination.

The analysis of 15+ strategic documents encompassed corporate strategy frameworks, existing technology roadmaps, innovation portfolios, quinquennial plans, and previous foresight exercises, uncovering significant gaps between strategic intent and operational execution. We supplemented this with a comprehensive survey of 44 participants across the organization to quantify perceptions of current foresight capabilities and identify priority improvement areas.

This diagnostic synthesis revealed five critical opportunity territories requiring intervention: strategic connection (linking corporate strategy with technology execution), integrated governance (overcoming organizational silos), actionable intelligence (transforming dispersed data into strategic insights), prospective methods (institutionalizing systematic foresight practices), and anticipatory mindsets (fostering future-oriented culture).

In parallel, we conducted a systematic benchmarking of 14 industry leaders across energy (Repsol, BP, Shell, Petrobras, TotalEnergies, Chevron), renewables (Iberdrola, Moeve, Oklo), and other sectors (NVIDIA, BASF, Enel, Bosch, Siemens), evaluating six core foresight capabilities: leadership & governance, environmental intelligence, future prospecting, vision & strategic direction, action & experimentation, and prospective culture. This analysis revealed that leading companies institutionalize foresight through CEO-level mandates, systematic environmental scanning, collaborative scenario development, and formal experimentation mechanisms—highlighting VTI's current "vulnerable" position requiring structured intervention across five opportunity territories.

We created and facilitated an intensive one-day co-creation workshop in Bogotá, bringing together 12 participants from VTI, business units, and strategic areas. The session began with inspirational framing on organizational purpose as "acts of hope that open future realities." Through structured collaborative dynamics, we co-created FARO's transformative purpose:

"We are the CT+I Lighthouse of prospective intelligence that connects the present with the technological future, enabling the Business Group to anticipate, interpret and act in high uncertainty environments."

We guided participants through systematic exploration of five strategic territories, generating 21 actionable initiatives across the opportunity dimensions. Applied the "Transition by Design" methodology to create an evolutionary three-version roadmap (V1-V3) starting from VTI's core influence areas and expanding progressively. Facilitated collaborative prioritization sessions using impact and stakeholder voting to identify highest-value initiatives for immediate implementation.

Then, we designed a comprehensive operating model structured around five integrated phases: Frame, Explore, Project, Define, and Transform. Developed detailed specifications for 10 priority initiatives across strategic territories, each with implementation requirements, responsible teams, dependencies, and success metrics. Created governance structure integrating Business Partners, ICPET, and business units with clear roles and decision-making processes.

Additionally, we developed a comprehensive FARO CT+I Foresight Toolkit—a practical guide that translates the theoretical model into actionable methodologies. This 50+ page playbook structures 20 specific tools across the five model phases, from stakeholder mapping and horizon scanning to scenario creation and design sprints, each with step-by-step instructions, templates, and downloadable resources. The toolkit serves as VTI's internal capability-building resource, enabling teams to apply foresight methodologies systematically while reducing dependence on external consultants.

Finally, we established a prioritized roadmap focusing on highest-impact initiatives: integrated strategy-technology model for synchronizing corporate strategy with technology execution, Executive Radar for continuous intelligence synthesis, and Intelligence Center for democratizing access to specialized information sources. Designed measurement system (FARO Impact Measurement) to demonstrate strategic value and guide continuous improvement.

04 —Result

Delivered a comprehensive foresight operating model that positions VTI as Ecopetrol's strategic technology anticipation hub, with demonstrated stakeholder alignment and clear implementation pathway. The FARO model provides systematic methodology for connecting long-term strategic vision with technology execution, featuring structured governance, continuous intelligence generation, and institutionalized prospective capabilities.

The collaborative process generated 10 actionable initiatives organized across five strategic territories, with clear prioritization and evolutionary roadmap spanning minimum viable model focused on digital technologies, expanded model incorporating emerging technologies, and consolidated model covering all critical Group technologies. Established governance structure with defined roles across planning, architecture, and innovation teams, supported by measurement systems and cultural transformation initiatives.

The co-creation approach ensured organizational buy-in through collaborative definition of purpose, priorities, and implementation approach. Six major reflections emerged:

  • Need for stronger technology-strategy connection
  • Evolution from reactive to continuous intelligence
  • Establishment of clear mandate overcoming fragmentation
  • Collaborative learning spaces
  • Tangible early results enabling escalation
  • Strengthened internal capabilities through common frameworks

Key learning: Successful technology foresight transformation requires simultaneous intervention across strategy alignment, governance structure, intelligence systems, methodological frameworks, and cultural change—achieved through collaborative co-creation that builds shared ownership and clear evolutionary pathway from core competencies toward comprehensive anticipation capabilities.

projects.sub: From Fragmented Portals to a Unified Experience

projects.html:
01 —Situation

The Bogotá Chamber of Commerce (CCB) is one of Colombia’s most influential business institutions, serving over 400,000 entrepreneurs and companies in the Bogotá region. It plays a central role in business formalization, economic development, and public-private collaboration. Over time, the CCB had developed more than 15 digital properties—including platforms, websites, and microsites—each managed independently by different departments or vendors. This resulted in a fragmented user experience, duplicated efforts, and limited ability to evolve strategically. In the context of broader institutional transformation, CCB set out to unify its digital ecosystem around a user-centered vision—improving access, strengthening brand coherence, and increasing operational efficiency.

02 —Task

I oversaw the project end to end, from crafting the commercial proposal and pitch to securing executive buy-in. Under my leadership, a multidisciplinary team led the research, experience strategy, and platform structuring. I took a hands-on role in critical phases—personally consolidating the governance model, designing key workflows and definitions, and presenting to CCB’s executive committee and president to achieve validation and approval. My goal was to ensure the institutional vision translated into a coherent, actionable, and future-ready framework.

03 —Action

Discovery & Ecosystem Diagnosis. We began with an in-depth diagnosis of CCB’s digital ecosystem through interviews, audits, platform analysis, and benchmarking. The team identified core issues: siloed decision-making, inconsistent user experiences, redundant services, and lack of shared standards. We mapped more than 15 active digital properties, 8 domains, and 21 distinct technology solutions—making the need for integration clear.

Experience Principles & Strategic Alignment. To guide future decisions, we defined six core experience principles—including Zero Friction, One CCB, and Make It Easy. These served as a north star for prioritizing content, structuring navigation, and reorganizing services. We developed user archetypes, journeys, decision trees, and service role models to align the future ecosystem with actual user needs.

Unified Structure for the Digital Ecosystem. We proposed a centralized, modular architecture that reorganized CCB’s digital presence into five main entry points: individual needs, business needs, procedures, highlighted services, and the business lifecycle. This future structure was validated through collaborative workshops and benchmark analysis. We delivered wireframes, information architecture, and a unified taxonomy to support implementation.

Governance Model Design. Building on the strategic vision, I consolidated and formalized a three-tier governance model—strategic, tactical, and operational—to clarify roles, streamline decisions, and sustain quality over time. I defined key governance processes, including intake workflows, “definition of ready,” and RACI matrices. I also led executive presentations to the organization’s leadership and secured endorsement from the president. The model provided CCB with a sustainable way to manage digital growth while maintaining consistency and accountability.

04 —Result

The project laid the foundation to transform a fragmented digital landscape into a coherent, user-centered, and governable ecosystem. The experience strategy enabled prioritization of key services and a structure rooted in real user needs. The governance model introduced clear ownership, cross-functional coordination, and mechanisms for sustained evolution. A key learning was that digital transformation isn’t just about platforms—it requires alignment between vision, operations, and organizational culture.

01 —Situation

MERAKI is a volunteer-driven initiative born from a leadership-in-transformation program. It brings together professionals in education, therapy, design, marketing, and fundraising to translate neuroscience and compassion into practical tools for early childhood development. Its anchor partner, Fundación Antioquia Infantil (FAIN), is launching a new campus in Caldas, Antioquia, to serve children and families in high-vulnerability contexts.

The goal: equip this site with inclusive, sensory-informed environments—participatory classrooms, a structured multisensory room, and adaptive spaces that support regulation, communication, play, and caregiver involvement. The broader ambition is to create a replicable model that integrates evidence-based design, early intervention, and community engagement for children aged 0–6, including those with developmental delays, autism spectrum conditions, or sensory processing challenges.

02 —Task

I initiated and led the conceptualization of MERAKI as a movement: a living system of sensory classrooms, practices, and communities rooted in neuroscience, compassion, and equity. I then assembled and mobilized a multidisciplinary team of volunteers—designers, therapists, educators, operational leads, and fundraisers—to bring it to life. As Project Lead, I drive the vision and strategy, structure the workstreams, and connect stakeholders across FAIN, vendors, donors, and the MERAKI team. I also ensure alignment to early childhood principles, lead resource mobilization, and define the playbooks and indicators that will guide future replications.

03 —Action

Conceptualization & Movement Framing. MERAKI began as a personal vision to bridge neuroscience and equity through design. I framed it not as a one-off intervention but as the seed of a larger system—a network of sensory classrooms adaptable to different territories and realities. This led to the creation of a modular model combining physical spaces, training protocols, and community activation. The conceptual backbone positioned MERAKI as a movement for sensory justice in early childhood.

Governance & Roadmap Integration. To operationalize the vision, we created a project structure with four synchronized streams—Infrastructure & Equipment, Educational Protocols, Communications & Fundraising, and Administration—coordinated through shared milestones and a weekly integration ritual. I established a phased roadmap, decision matrices, and a lightweight dashboard to monitor progress, risks, and impact.

Infrastructure & Equipment. In collaboration with FAIN therapists and educators, we designed spatial programs aligned to sensory goals—zoning, lighting, acoustics, and flow. Equipment was selected to support vestibular, tactile, proprioceptive, and auditory stimulation.

Educational Component & Training. We kicked off with a neuroeducation-led workshop for FAIN staff, grounding sensory integration in everyday practice. From there, we co-designed training modules on observing child responses, pacing sensory input, and designing adaptive routines.

Communications & Fundraising. To mobilize support, we created a social-driven fundraising strategy blending digital storytelling, small individual pledges, and corporate in-kind support. Two flagship events—a neuroeducation training and a music fundraiser in Medellín—helped expand reach and generate visibility. A funnel-based dashboard tracks outreach, engagement, and donation fulfillment, driving weekly optimizations.

04 —Result

In early 2026, FAIN’s Caldas campus will open with a fully equipped sensory learning ecosystem projected to benefit 200+ children per year, plus their caregivers. The space translates neuroscience into daily interactions—supporting attention, communication, emotional regulation, and motor coordination through inclusive design.

Educators and families gain simple, repeatable strategies that extend from the classroom into the home. The Caldas pilot establishes the first node in a larger vision: a MERAKI network of sensory spaces, rooted in equity, science, and care—positioned to scale across new communities in the years ahead.

01 —Context

Ecopetrol, a prominent energy company in Latin America, sought to optimize its cash flow management amidst the volatile global energy market and the transition to sustainable practices. Effective cash flow management is crucial for Ecopetrol to navigate price fluctuations, demand changes, and support growth and sustainability. The Vice Presidency of Finance and the Hub at EBA aimed to enhance financial processes and outcomes through the 360° Cash Flow initiative, leveraging advanced analytics and technology.

02 —Challenge

The main challenge was to shift from traditional, production-focused cash flow analysis to a proactive, value-oriented model. Ecopetrol needed a robust system that could provide real-time insights, streamline data capture, and improve the accuracy of financial projections. This transformation required overcoming existing operational inefficiencies and integrating innovative technological solutions.

03 —The Process

The project began with a focused planning phase where we defined the strategic goals and assembled a multidisciplinary team. Key stakeholders were interviewed to capture pain points and aspirations, laying the groundwork for a collaborative and informed design process.

With this foundation, we moved into the exploration and alignment phase. Together, we constructed a shared knowledge base, allowing participants to map out the challenge and clarify the long-term objectives. This created the conditions for collective understanding and a unified vision.

From there, we entered a highly creative ideation stage. Using structured co-creation sessions, the team generated a broad array of ideas, exploring diverse ways to enhance cash flow management. These ideas were progressively refined through sketches and discussions until a cohesive concept emerged.

Decision-making followed, where we prioritized the most viable ideas and began to shape the user experience. A high-level prototype flow was created, supported by detailed screen designs that illustrated how the platform would function.

Next came the prototyping stage. We developed a realistic, interactive prototype and designed a storytelling script to demonstrate the solution’s potential. This prototype showcased key features like liquidity position tracking, projection tools, and simulation capabilities.

Finally, the prototype was tested with financial experts and stakeholders. Their feedback was instrumental in identifying opportunities for improvement and ensuring that the solution addressed real-world needs effectively.

04 —Results

The 360° Cash Flow prototype introduced a new way of managing finances at Ecopetrol. It offered intuitive tools for scenario simulation, cash flow visualization, and strategic planning—empowering teams to move from reactive analysis to proactive insight. The Design Sprint led to several key advancements:

  1. Prototype Development: Created a functional prototype for a 360° Cash Flow platform, featuring intuitive tools for exploring, filtering, and analyzing financial data. Key features included liquidity position, cash projection, cash flow simulation, performance tracking, and optimization.
  2. User-Centered Solutions: Validated the prototype with stakeholders, ensuring it met user needs and addressed key pain points. The tools facilitated a more efficient, data-driven decision-making process, reducing manual tasks and improving data clarity.
  3. Strategic Alignment: Aligned the new tools with Ecopetrol’s strategic goals, supporting a more structured and systematic approach to cash flow analysis and macroeconomic forecasting. This alignment enabled better integration of expert knowledge, analytical models, and external data sources.
  4. Enhanced Collaboration: Fostered a collaborative culture among team members, combining diverse perspectives to innovate and solve complex problems. Stakeholder involvement was crucial for achieving buy-in and support for the new initiatives.

05 —Impact

This initiative transformed cash flow management at Ecopetrol. The platform enabled real-time insights, reduced manual data handling, and improved forecast accuracy. It also supported strategic decision-making with simulation and optimization tools. Beyond the technical benefits, the project fostered a cultural shift toward agility, user-centered thinking, and innovation—laying the groundwork for a smarter, more resilient financial future.

In October 2024, Ecopetrol, in partnership with The Cocktail, CCCS, and XM, held a co-creation workshop in Bogotá. The objective was to explore opportunities to reuse byproducts from the oil and gas industry in sustainable construction, following the principles of Circular Economy. Ecopetrol faced challenges related to making these materials (e.g., spent catalysts, clarification solids, and construction and demolition waste) commercially viable and sustainable for the construction and infrastructure sectors.

02 —The Challenge

The challenge was to create a sustainable and circular business model that would allow the certification and commercialization of byproducts generated in Ecopetrol's operations. The difficulty lay in bringing together different actors in the ecosystem—regulatory bodies, construction companies, and strategic allies—while ensuring technical feasibility, market acceptance, and regulatory compliance.

03 —What We Did

  • Facilitated a co-creation workshop using agile methodologies at The Cocktail Bogotá.
  • Engaged teams from CCCS and XM, along with science, technology, and innovation experts from Ecopetrol.
  • Identified and prioritized key byproducts for circular exploration: clarification solids, spent FCC catalysts, construction waste, and modified asphalt.
  • Developed business model prototypes focusing on the reuse of these byproducts.
  • Explored application areas, including public infrastructure, social housing, and commercial construction projects.
  • Established synergies and alliances to enable pilot projects.
  • Documented the results and outlined next steps for scaling the model.

04 —The Impact

  • Identified 5 key application areas for byproducts in infrastructure and construction.
  • Developed business model prototypes focused on reusing clarification solids and FCC catalysts.
  • Explored strategic alliances across sectors to support certification and commercialization of byproducts.
  • Inspiration and alignment among participants, fostering future collaborations for sustainable operations.

05 —After this project

At VML, we developed a venture-building project with Ecopetrol to launch a new business unit focused on finding circular solutions for byproducts of their production processes.

At Ecopetrol's refineries, water from the Magdalena River must be clarified before entering the production cycle, leaving behind solid matter that was previously treated as waste. At Neture Impact (part of VML), we helped Ecopetrol transform this byproduct into sustainable bricks, turning what once was discarded material into a valuable commercial solution for the construction industry.

01 —Context

Parque Explora, a renowned science museum in Medellín, Colombia, embarked on a strategic transformation journey to enhance its impact on the community and ensure long-term sustainability. The organization aimed to integrate its diverse offerings, including interactive exhibitions, educational programs, and conservation efforts, into a cohesive strategic framework. This initiative was driven by the need to align internal processes, foster a unified organizational culture, and leverage technological advancements for greater operational efficiency.

02 —The Challenge

Parque Explora had reached an inflection point: rapid growth and diversification created strong momentum, while also revealing an opportunity to clarify strategic direction and strengthen shared organizational practices. Over time, operations had become more complex and fragmented, leading to misaligned priorities, process inefficiencies, and moments where focus on the museum’s core mission became diluted. In parallel, advancing a sustainable financial model and deepening stakeholder engagement became critical to securing long-term viability.

03 —My Role

I led the end-to-end development of the commercial proposal, from shaping a winning value proposition to delivering client presentations and negotiating project scope. Once the engagement was initiated, I guided the consulting team by providing strategic direction, contextual insights about Parque Explora, and depth of analysis. I also shaped the impact narrative aligned with global future trends and refined the operational model to ensure coherence between vision and execution.

04 —The Process

We began with a comprehensive diagnostic to understand the current state of the organization. This included over 50 internal documents, 20 interviews with leadership, and two focus groups with frontline teams and community members. A physical site visit provided insight into the spatial and operational realities of the museum. This phase revealed deep misalignment between teams, disconnected initiatives, and a lack of shared strategic language.

Through collaborative workshops, we surfaced core tensions and aspirations. We identified four global forces shaping the future—planetary health, technological acceleration, social justice, and globalization—which became the foundation for strategic sensemaking. We facilitated the alignment of leadership around a bold but grounded purpose: to catalyze social and environmental transformation through knowledge, curiosity, and participation.

We co-created a new strategic architecture with leadership: a shared purpose, one organizational objective, and four impact pillars—Augmented Curiosity, Active Citizenship, Relevant Schools, and Conscious Conservation. These pillars connected Explora’s diverse programs to global futures and local realities. We also articulated a dual-operating model—museum and project development hub—and introduced the metaphor of a “cultural ecotone” to describe the synergy between both worlds.

We translated the strategy into a transformation roadmap built around four strategic fronts: Strategic Deployment, Cultural Harmony, Operational Symphony, and Path to the Future. Each front included a set of high-leverage initiatives—such as cultural transformation, interoperability architecture, and a new sustainability model—each designed to bridge the gap between vision and execution.

These strategic definitions provide a comprehensive framework for Parque Explora to navigate future challenges, ensuring the alignment of its operations with its mission and goals, while fostering a culture of learning, collaboration, and sustainability.

05 —Result

The project delivered Parque Explora’s first formal corporate strategy, fully co-created and approved by its leadership team. It established a strategic operating system that aligns its dual identities—museum and innovation partner—and positions it as a catalyst for collective learning and transformation. Personally, the project deepened my practice in strategic foresight, cultural systems design, and public innovation—reinforcing design as a driver of systemic change.

01 —Context

En Tu Hogar is a strategic initiative led by KOF - TCCC to establish a renewed vision and strategic roadmap for Coca-Cola’s D2C (Direct-to-Consumer) channel in Mexico. The project aims to consolidate a strategic plan that provides focus and direction for future actions, leveraging the largest areas of opportunity and addressing key challenges to become a reference for the digital channel D2C. The initial goal is to transform the way Coca-Cola interacts with its customers through a robust and scalable digital ecosystem.

Coca-Cola En tu Hogar holds a cherished place in Mexican culture, evoking nostalgia and shared family moments. Its broad product range, affordability, and accessibility have solidified its iconic status across generations.

However, in a crowded market dominated by fast-delivery and pure-digital players, this legacy alone is insufficient. The channel faces low awareness and lacks a distinct value proposition, hindering its ability to compete effectively and retain customers.

02 —The Challenge

Coca-Cola FEMSA and The Coca-Cola Company set out to redefine the strategic direction of their direct-to-consumer (D2C) channel in Mexico, known as Coca-Cola en Tu Hogar (CCETH). Despite a 19% year-over-year revenue increase and a growing digital customer base, the channel faced major challenges: a fragmented value proposition, limited differentiation, and internal gaps that hindered scalability. The goal was to align both organizations around a bold, actionable vision and build the strategic foundations for CCETH to become a $1.5B business by 2028.

03 —The Process

Immersion: Understanding the ecosystem and identifying blind spots. We began with a rapid yet thorough immersion phase, analyzing over 24 internal documents from KOF and KO, reviewing past initiatives, and conducting steering sessions with executive stakeholders. This allowed us to map the ecosystem holistically and surface inconsistencies between the formal strategy and the lived experience of users and teams. Through this “reality check,” we uncovered critical gaps in customer segmentation, service consistency, and digital readiness.

Exploration: Stakeholder dialogue and user research. The exploration phase combined over 25 stakeholder interviews with 1:1 user interviews and co-creation activities. We engaged decision-makers across marketing, tech, and operations to understand their strategic ambitions, and brought in direct voices from customers to validate value perceptions. We then facilitated a strategic thinking workshop in Mexico City with leaders from KO and KOF, where we used visual frameworks to connect business intent with user expectations.

Diagnosis: Six strategic dimensions. We synthesized our findings across six dimensions—customer, competition, financials, platform, organizational structure, and corporate alignment—to form a diagnosis of the current state. This analysis revealed a D2C model struggling to deliver consistency and emotional connection in its digital experience. We mapped proto-personas (e.g., single moms, digital planners, modern families) and tied them to unmet needs across the experience journey—from delivery to loyalty to product variety.

Defining capabilities and competitive advantage. Next, we framed six growth enablers to make the value proposition tangible: Home Attraction, Customer Experience, Portfolio Development, Data Strategy, Route-to-Market, and Organizational Transformation. We mapped capability gaps and surfaced where KOF and KO were aligned—and where they weren’t. This insight helped us design a two-phase transformation model: "Fix the Basics" to stabilize operations and "Value to Home" to scale and differentiate.

Strategic framing and prioritization. In the final definition stage, we translated the vision into a clear, phased roadmap. Each capability was broken down into strategic initiatives that addressed the most urgent business needs—improving delivery reliability, expanding the product portfolio, and designing a loyalty model rooted in emotional and financial value. We developed an executive narrative and visual model to communicate how CCETH could evolve from a transactional service into a distinctive, scalable relationship platform.

04 —Task

As Strategic Design Lead, I guided the exploration from a customer-centric and systems-thinking perspective. I facilitated key stakeholder engagements, synthesized insights from multiple data streams, and translated findings into strategic frameworks and opportunity areas. I also led the articulation of the strategic narrative that shaped our final definition of capabilities, growth drivers, and roadmap priorities.

05 —Result

The project delivered a shared strategic vision, a prioritized roadmap, and a set of actionable growth drivers that both KOF and KO adopted as the foundation for the next evolution of the D2C channel. These definitions have informed subsequent investment decisions and served as the north star for digital, portfolio, and organizational transformation. For me, this project sharpened my ability to design in complexity—balancing user insight, business logic, and systemic change—while facilitating alignment across diverse executive audiences.

projects.html:
This project was an academic exercise from the course "Introduction to Futures Design" at CENTRO.

01 —Context

Mexico City (CDMX) faces a growing threat from climate change, manifested in droughts, floods, and extreme temperatures. Socioeconomic inequality and lack of access to basic services exacerbate the situation. In this context, a foresight workshop was conducted to design possible and resilient futures for CDMX in 2050, aiming to anticipate and mitigate the adverse effects of climate change and climate gentrification.

02 —The Challenge

The main challenge was to address the multiple problems that CDMX faces due to climate change and growing inequality. These include water scarcity, climate migration, air pollution, and social exclusion caused by climate gentrification. It was crucial to find inclusive and sustainable solutions that would allow the city to adapt to an uncertain and adverse future.

03 —The Method

The project utilized a comprehensive foresight methodology involving horizon scanning to identify emerging trends and signals of change, trend mapping to understand key influences on the city's future, and the application of Dator's Futures Archetypes to explore diverse scenarios such as continuation, collapse, discipline, and transformation. Detailed scenarios were created, including the "Walled Oasis," to visualize potential outcomes. The desired future state was defined with a focus on resilience, inclusivity, and sustainability.

04 —"Walled Oasis" Scenario

The "Walled Oasis" scenario presents a thought-provoking and dystopian vision of Mexico City (CDMX) in 2050, highlighting the complex interplay between climate resilience and social inequality. This scenario serves as a powerful narrative to explore the potential consequences of unchecked climate change and the socio-economic dynamics it could exacerbate.

In this imagined future, certain areas of CDMX have evolved into "oasis" zones characterized by highly adaptable and resilient infrastructure. These zones have benefitted from significant public and private investments, transforming them into urban havens capable of withstanding extreme climate events. However, this prosperity comes with a high cost: the intensification of social exclusion through climate gentrification. Here are some implications:

  • Social Exclusion: The scenario starkly illustrates how efforts to adapt to climate change can inadvertently lead to greater social exclusion if not managed inclusively. The fortified oases become enclaves of privilege, leaving the less affluent to struggle with worsening environmental conditions.
  • Urban Fragmentation: The physical and social barriers created by the wall reinforce segregation, leading to a fragmented urban landscape where opportunities and resources are unevenly distributed.
  • Tensions and Conflicts: The scenario hints at the potential for increased social tensions and conflicts as disparities grow more pronounced, with the fortified zones symbolizing a failure to achieve equitable resilience.

05 —The Concept: Center for Climate Resilience

The Climate Resilience Center (CRC) represents a forward-thinking and inclusive approach to tackling the multifaceted challenges posed by climate change in Mexico City (CDMX). Conceived as a beacon of hope and a hub for innovation, the CRC aims to foster a more resilient and equitable urban environment by promoting collaboration, research, and action against climate change and its socio-economic impacts.

Vision and Mission

The CRC aspires to a future where CDMX thrives in a context of participatory climate resilience. It envisions a society where academia, public institutions, private sectors, and communities work together to forge equitable solutions to climate challenges. The center's mission emphasizes accessibility, inclusiveness, and the democratization of climate knowledge, striving to ensure that all citizens benefit from its initiatives.

Key Features

  1. Collaborative Research: The CRC facilitates cutting-edge research in climate science, focusing on practical solutions that can be implemented in urban settings. It encourages collaboration between scientists, policymakers, and community leaders to address local climate issues effectively.
  2. Education and Training: The center offers extensive training programs and workshops aimed at building capacity among residents, professionals, and policymakers. These initiatives focus on climate literacy, sustainable practices, and innovative adaptation strategies.
  3. Policy Advocacy: By engaging in political advocacy, the CRC seeks to influence public policies and promote regulations that support climate resilience and social equity. It acts as a voice for vulnerable communities, ensuring their needs and perspectives are considered in decision-making processes.
  4. Public Awareness and Outreach: The CRC is dedicated to raising public awareness about the impacts of climate change and the importance of resilience. Through campaigns, seminars, and community events, it aims to foster a culture of proactive adaptation and environmental stewardship.
  5. Innovation Hub: The center serves as an incubator for climate-related innovations and entrepreneurial initiatives. It supports startups and projects that offer sustainable solutions to urban challenges, providing resources and mentorship to turn ideas into impactful actions.
  6. Temporary Refuge for Climate Migrants: Recognizing the growing issue of climate-induced migration, the CRC provides temporary shelter and support services for climate migrants. This initiative ensures that migrants have access to essential resources and integration programs.

01 —The Context

The Fundación Botánica y Zoológica de Barranquilla (ZooBaq), a longstanding science and conservation institution in Colombia's Caribbean region, faced urgent challenges of public relevance, infrastructure decay, and digital obsolescence. Amid shifting global expectations around animal welfare, conservation, and visitor engagement, ZooBaq sought to define a compelling vision for its future. The goal: to craft a strategic roadmap that would enable the organization to thrive as a regional science center and biodiversity hub.

02 —The Task

As Strategic Design Lead at The Cocktail LATAM, I led the design and facilitation of a WorkShot (strategy workshop) focused on aligning leadership around a shared vision and defining key priorities for organizational transformation. My role involved orchestrating systemic analysis, synthesizing collective aspirations, and translating complexity into actionable design directions and strategic opportunities.

03 —The Process

We convened a two-day strategic WorkShot with ZooBaq’s executive team to co-create their future trajectory. Using The Cocktail’s proprietary frameworks, we mapped the organization's current strategic dimensions—purpose, value proposition, communities, capabilities, and resources—and contrasted them with its future aspirations.

Through participatory methods, we surfaced six systemic challenges (e.g., infrastructural uncertainty, loss of public relevance, and fragmented digital experience) and developed corresponding transformation priorities.

The output included a roadmap with five strategic fronts: public positioning, infrastructure renovation, financial sustainability through service activation, digital transformation, and operational clarity. Each stream was detailed with objectives, enablers, barriers, and key initiatives, enabling the institution to align action with mission.

A core component of the process was a foresight exercise where participants envisioned ZooBaq’s long-term role in the conservation of the Caribbean region. This included co-defining a “North Star” vision and exploring plausible future scenarios around infrastructure, community engagement, and sustainability. These scenario explorations helped identify strategic tensions and informed the creation of a phased roadmap responsive to both current constraints and future possibilities.

01 —Context

AFORE Coppel, a prominent pension fund administrator in Mexico, plays a critical role in managing retirement resources for millions of workers. Despite progress in the pension system, many affiliates face challenges in securing sufficient funds for a complete pension upon retirement. This strategic initiative aimed to identify opportunities to increase member engagement and contributions, ultimately improving pension outcomes.

02 —Challenge

AFORE Coppel faced significant challenges:

  • Demographics and Contribution Patterns: Nearly 50% of affiliates are under 35, earning between 1 and 3 minimum wages, with sporadic contributions due to unstable or informal employment.
  • Inactive Members: Approximately 70% of affiliates are inactive, not making regular contributions, putting them at risk of not securing a complete pension.
  • Financial Literacy: A lack of financial education and awareness among members limits their engagement and understanding of the benefits of consistent contributions.

03 —Methodology

Systemic Immersion. Conducted an in-depth analysis of the entire lifecycle of an AFORE Coppel affiliate, from initial awareness to receiving their pension. Identified key enablers and inhibitors affecting member engagement and contribution behaviors.

Strategic Definition and Opportunity Identification. Defined clear intentions to support affiliates from their first contribution through to their final pension payment with transparency, information, and education. Identified eight key opportunity areas for intervention, including activation, training, internal structure, customer learning, leveraging Coppel's ecosystem, loyalty programs, present-day improvements, and communication.

Ideation and Solution Development. Brainstormed and prioritized a range of initiatives to address identified challenges, focusing on both internal processes and external member engagement. Developed detailed proposals for initiatives with the most potential impact.

04 —Core Impact Areas

  1. Increased Member Engagement: Boost regular contributions by improving awareness of the benefits of formal employment and consistent savings.
  2. Enhanced Financial Literacy: Provide comprehensive financial education to empower members with better saving habits and informed decision-making.
  3. Operational Efficiency: Streamline processes and integrate data to improve internal workflows and customer service efficiency.
  4. Sustainable Saving Practices: Promote voluntary savings and reward good financial behaviors through innovative programs and incentives.
  5. Social Inclusion and Formal Employment: Support inactive and informal workers in transitioning to formal employment, increasing their chances of securing a full pension.
  6. Improved Customer Experience: Enhance the overall member experience with personalized support, clear information, and responsive service throughout their savings journey.
  7. Strengthened Community Trust: Foster a sense of belonging and trust among affiliates towards AFORE Coppel, enhancing loyalty and long-term engagement.

01 —The Context

Ecopetrol, a leading energy company in Latin America, embarked on a strategic initiative to enhance its financial asset management processes. The company's long-term strategy, "Energy that Transforms," aims to address environmental, social, and governance challenges, creating sustainable value for its stakeholders. The Vice Presidency of Finance and the Hub at EBA sought to develop analytical models supported by technological solutions to improve asset planning and management, aligning with the company's strategic objectives.

02 —The Challenge

The primary challenge faced by Ecopetrol was the transformation of its financial asset management conversations. Traditionally focused on past performance and accountability, the goal was to shift towards maximizing future value and a 360-degree perspective. This required overcoming entrenched practices and assumptions, and adopting new, agile methodologies that could foster innovation and user-centered solutions.

03 —The Process

  1. Planning and Preparation: Defined the challenge and objectives for the sprint. Selected a multidisciplinary core team and planned activities for the sprint week. Gathered relevant information and conducted stakeholder interviews to understand the context.
  2. Understanding and Defining: Conducted structured discussions to create a shared knowledge base among participants. Mapped out the challenge and defined the long-term goals and key questions to address.
  3. Ideation and Sketching: Facilitated exercises to generate and refine a wide range of ideas. Developed detailed sketches of potential solutions.

  5. Prototyping: Developed a realistic prototype of the chosen solution. Designed and defined a script for presenting the concept and functionalities.
  6. Validation: Tested the prototype with five key stakeholders. Collected feedback to identify strengths and opportunities for improvement.

04 —Impact

The Design Sprint led to significant advancements in Ecopetrol's asset management approach:

  • Prototype Development: Created a functional prototype that facilitated real-time visualization of financial data, allowing managers to make informed decisions based on current and projected performance metrics.
  • User-Centered Solutions: Validated the prototype with stakeholders, ensuring the solution met user needs and addressed key pain points, such as reducing manual processes and enhancing data-driven decision-making.
  • Strategic Alignment: Aligned the new tool with Ecopetrol's long-term strategy, enabling a more proactive and predictive approach to asset management.
  • Enhanced Collaboration: Fostered a collaborative culture among team members, combining diverse perspectives to innovate and solve complex problems.

This Design Sprint not only transformed the financial asset management processes at Ecopetrol but also set a precedent for future innovation projects, highlighting the value of agile methodologies and user-centered design in driving organizational change.

projects.excerpt: Empathy & Immersion. Next, we invited educators to step into the shoes of their students. Through a guided imagination exercise, they mapped classroom experiences from a learner’s perspective—observing behaviors,…
projects.html:
01 —Situation — The Challenge

As part of the Juntos Aprendemos program, and in collaboration with Parque Explora, we set out to support teachers and school leaders in Antioquia navigating post-pandemic challenges. Many classrooms had remained static despite mounting technological, social, and educational shifts. Educators were looking for ways to re-engage students and reinvent learning experiences. Our workshop aimed to spark this transformation through small but powerful interventions—“hacks”—to reimagine the classroom as a dynamic, participatory space for learning in the 21st century.

02 —Task — My Role

I led the initiative as Head of Innovation, co-designing and facilitating the virtual workshop in partnership with the Parque Explora team. I developed the workshop structure, infused it with creative methodologies, and hosted the session with over 300 educators. My focus was on guiding participants through a process of reflection, ideation, and prototyping, creating a space for connection, creativity, and shared learning across regions.

03 —Action — The Process

Discovery & Intention Setting. We opened the session by surfacing shared intentions: What makes a learning experience memorable? Using collaborative tools like Mentimeter, participants defined their own “EMA” (experiencia memorable de aprendizaje), forming the foundation for their design challenges.

Empathy & Immersion. Next, we invited educators to step into the shoes of their students. Through a guided imagination exercise, they mapped classroom experiences from a learner’s perspective—observing behaviors, emotions, and interactions to surface unmet needs and opportunities.

Hack Ideation & Design. Inspired by prompts (e.g., “How might we reconfigure the classroom for different learning styles?”), participants proposed tangible hacks—from project-based learning to spatial reorganization and intercultural exchange. Using Padlet, they shared, commented on, and iterated ideas in real time, building a collective repository of prototypes and inspiration.

Storytelling & Reflection. To close, participants authored short narrative pieces—“love letters” to their future classrooms—connecting their intentions to their proposed interventions. The session ended with a shared reflection on how small actions can generate systemic change in education.

04 —Result — The Impact

The workshop reached over 300 educators across Antioquia, fostering creative dialogue and new connections within a community still recovering from the pandemic. While designed as a sensitization exercise, it activated a mindset of experimentation and empowered teachers to see themselves as agents of transformation. A key takeaway: systemic change can begin with small, intentional hacks—especially when grounded in empathy and shared purpose.

projects.title: Planetario de Medellín
projects.sub: Renewal Strategy
projects.excerpt: Concept Development. Based on the research, we developed the core narrative: “Our Place in the Universe”—not just as a scientific inquiry, but as a human and existential one. We defined two guiding horizons: Origins…
projects.html:
01 —Situation

After a decade of operations, the Planetario de Medellín needed a major renewal to stay relevant in a changing cultural and educational landscape. Its original museographic offer, focused mainly on astronomy, no longer resonated with increasingly diverse and critical audiences. The challenge was not only to modernize infrastructure and content, but to reframe the planetarium as a space for existential reflection, interdisciplinary dialogue, and inclusive public engagement—positioning science as both a tool for wonder and a catalyst for planetary responsibility.

02 —Task

I served as Head of Innovation and led the museography team throughout the conceptualization and experience design process. My role included guiding the creative and strategic vision, facilitating interdisciplinary workshops, and ensuring coherence between the scientific, cultural, and spatial dimensions of the visitor experience. I worked closely with educators, scientists, designers, and community stakeholders to craft an exhibition that invites critical thinking and emotional connection.

03 —Action

Discovery & Strategic Framing. We began with an extensive participatory research phase: surveys with over 200 visitors and non-visitors, stakeholder interviews, focus groups with educators and community leaders, and internal ideation sessions. This helped us surface deep user insights—especially the need to move beyond hard science into more human, emotional, and philosophical territory.

Concept Development. Based on the research, we developed the core narrative: “Our Place in the Universe”—not just as a scientific inquiry, but as a human and existential one. We defined two guiding horizons: Origins (where we come from) and Edges (what lies beyond), to anchor content and spatial storytelling. This narrative was built to provoke wonder, decentralize Western perspectives, and reintroduce visitors to themselves as cosmic citizens.

Experience Co-Design. We led multiple co-creation workshops with Explora staff, astronomers, artists, accessibility advocates, and teachers to define multi-sensory, inclusive experiences. This process emphasized interaction beyond the visual—through sound, tactility, posture, and narrative—to make science accessible and meaningful for all audiences, including children, older adults, and people with disabilities.

Spatial and Narrative Integration. My team worked on translating abstract concepts into immersive spatial experiences. We developed a sequence across three floors—from Earth’s biodiversity to cosmic scale—using design tools like interactive constellations, planetary distance markers, and a large-scale mural of cosmic history. Each zone balanced scientific depth with artistic storytelling and emotional resonance.

04 —Result

The resulting proposal redefined the Planetarium not just as a science venue, but as a cultural space for critical reflection and collective imagination. It introduced new forms of accessibility, multisensory engagement, and narrative depth that were previously missing. A key takeaway: when designing for science, grounding complexity in human emotion and local context can create deeper, more transformative public experiences.

01 —Context

The project focuses on the renovation and revitalization of the Memory Station Museum in Puerto Colombia, a place with a rich history of migration and cultural development. Puerto Colombia, known for its historic pier and railway station, has been a crucial entry point to the country and a hub of cultural and economic exchanges since the 19th century.

In 2022 Parque Explora was selected to design the museum’s next chapter through a comprehensive Master Planning effort aiming to consolidate a museum for the public engagement of the history of the port —its migrants and settlers, the dock and its daily life, the station and the railway—, and the mark that this milestone left on the culture of Puerto Colombia and the transformation of Colombia.

02 —The Challenge

The main challenge was to understand and document the needs and perceptions of the local community and visitors regarding the museum's revitalization. The goal was to identify the most relevant historical and cultural elements, as well as opportunities to improve the museum's infrastructure and cultural offerings, ensuring its sustainability and relevance in the current context.

Through stories and living memories, embedded in objects, archive documents, family albums, remains of infrastructure, and current elements of the mix of cultures, visitors will immerse themselves in the past and present of a place that was the gateway to the transformation of the country and that today is projected as a symbol of conscious development, sustainable and human.

03 —What We Did

  • Document Review: An extensive analysis of Puerto Colombia's history and heritage, as well as local and national development plans.
  • Site Visits: Visits to the site to better understand its current state and potential.
  • Interviews and Workshops: Organized interviews with key stakeholders and co-creation workshops with community members and experts to gather diverse perspectives and build a shared vision for the project.
  • Contextual Analysis: Diagnoses were developed on the normative state and needs of the local population, considering social, economic, and cultural factors.

The results of this diagnostic phase enabled:

  • Identification of Challenges and Opportunities: Key aspects were highlighted, such as the importance of including diverse communities and enhancing the living heritage of Puerto Colombia.
  • Foundation for Project Design: Ideas and proposals for museographic and urban intervention were consolidated, aligned with the community's needs and expectations.
  • Community Engagement: Active participation from Puerto Colombia residents generated a sense of ownership and support for the project, crucial for its future success and sustainability.

04 —The Proposal

  • Design of Interactive Experiences: Proposed new narratives and interactive formats, integrating digital and physical media to enrich the visitor experience.
  • Architectural Intervention: Planned the renovation of the station and the construction of new spaces, such as a multipurpose pavilion and a connecting pergola, to unify the different elements of the site.
  • Expanded Museography: Proposed extending the museum experience beyond its walls with installations and signage in the plaza and pier, creating an accessible and attractive cultural route.
  • Sustainability and Management: Designed strategies to ensure the long-term economic and operational viability of the museum, including seeking partnerships and funding.

05 —Intended Impact

  • Heritage Revitalization: The proposed intervention aims to value and preserve Puerto Colombia's cultural heritage, turning the museum into a reference for local history and identity.
  • Inclusion and Community Participation: Involving various voices in the project's design and planning strengthens the sense of ownership and collaboration between the community and the museum.
  • Tourism and Cultural Attraction: The museum's renovation and expansion position Puerto Colombia as a prominent tourist and cultural destination, boosting the local economy and fostering sustainable development.
  • Educational Innovation: Creating educational and participatory experiences enriches the museum's cultural and educational offerings, benefiting students and visitors of all ages.
